description:
MedVital: an onboard doctor for deep space. Mars is up to 20 min from Earth, so astronauts must catch their own health problems. We're building an app that tracks heart, sleep, radiation and mood, with offline AI that flags changes and tells the crew what to do.

I'm Carl (City Tech, CUNY) on backend + AI. We need data/viz, front-end/UI, a pitch lead and bio/health minds.

Beginners welcome. If you're motivated and want to ship something real in 48 hours, join us at NYU Tandon or online.
summary: MedVital is a software-based astronaut health monitoring system designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to mitigate radiation, bone loss, cardiovascular anomalies, and behavioral health risks. The solution features a simulated screenless wearable that continuously tracks astronaut vitals without interfering with spacesuits. These telemetry bursts are transmitted every five seconds to a localized spacecraft hub powered by a Cloudflare Worker and D1 edge database. The edge-computing hub operates independently of Earth, comparing live data against individual pre-flight baselines. If severe anomalies or space weather events are detected, the system bypasses visual screens and issues haptic vibration alerts directly to the wrist, like three buzzes for immediate radiation danger. Crucially, MedVital guarantees zero data loss during deep space communication blackouts. When the link drops, the onboard network queues all records locally. Once connectivity is restored, it automatically batch-syncs the entire history to the NASA mission control receiver. The simulation is grounded in authentic scientific data, actively integrating the NASA DONKI, Curiosity RAD, and OSDR datasets to ensure maximum operational realism
details:
Why MedVital stands out

  1. Help in seconds, not 44 minutes. The astronaut asks the on-board assistant and gets an answer built from their own live numbers and their own pre-flight baseline. If it is serious, Send to flight surgeon puts the whole conversation on the NASA screen at once.
  2. Nothing is lost when the link drops. In the demo you press Cut the link: Cloudflare turns red, a 3-2-1 retry counter runs, and records wait safely in the database. Press Restore and they rush to NASA back to back, then a checker confirms the three databases agree.
  3. A research record, not just a dashboard. Sleep, spacewalks, onboard tests, radiation dose and alerts are kept per astronaut for the whole mission and sent to NASA, so one mission's data can inform the next.
  4. A wearable built around its battery and a network built around trust. The wearable does almost nothing on purpose, and every connection to the spacecraft goes through a private, secret-key network.

The problem

On a trip to Mars, a radio signal takes roughly 3 to 22 minutes to cross the gap in one direction, depending on where the planets are. A question to flight control and its answer can take 6 to 44 minutes round trip. The link can also drop entirely: when Mars is on the far side of the Sun, communication can be interrupted for about two weeks.

Now picture what an astronaut may face in that gap: a racing heart, a headache, poor sleep, or a solar storm on its way while they are outside the spacecraft. Radiation, bone loss, heart strain and behavioral health are exactly the risks that build up over a long mission, and they cannot wait for a reply from Earth.

MedVital moves first-line health support on board. Every reading is checked against that astronaut's own pre-flight report, an on-board assistant answers right away, and anything serious goes to the flight surgeon with one tap. Whatever the link does, every record reaches NASA.

What MedVital does

MedVital is fully software and covers four or more astronaut health risks: radiation, bone, heart and behavioral health (sleep and stress).

  1. Baseline first. Before the mission, each astronaut's pre-flight medical report is loaded in, so the system knows what is normal for that person. Without a baseline, readings could be far off.
  2. The wearable reads and reports. It tracks heart rate, blood oxygen, breathing, temperature, sleep and radiation dose, and sends small bursts to the spacecraft. The astronaut never has to touch it.
  3. The spacecraft hub does the thinking. It compares every reading with the astronaut's own baseline. Fixed rules decide when to alert, and the AI explains the alert in plain language, for example: "There is a solar event right now. You have reached X% of your radiation limit for this spacewalk. Head back in."
  4. The astronaut gets help right away. The wearable vibrates with a different pattern for each alert type (below), and the on-board assistant answers questions from the astronaut's own screen.
  5. Everything goes back to NASA. Alerts, daily summaries and reports travel over the link to Earth. If the link drops, records wait on the spacecraft and rush to NASA when it returns.
  • RETURN_NOW (radiation or a solar event): 3 long buzzes, repeating until the astronaut is back inside.
  • CHECK_VITALS (heart rate or blood oxygen off baseline): 2 short buzzes.
  • INFO (daily summary or exercise reminder ready): 1 short buzz.

The spacewalk moment. The astronaut presses Leave the spacecraft and the radiation level on the screen starts to climb. After a certain amout of time the screen shows "Go back inside by ..." with a countdown. Ignore it, and the screen turns red, the wearable buzzes, and the only option left is Go back inside. The time outside and the dose received are recorded under Spacewalks and sent to NASA.

Design choices

A wearable that does almost nothing, on purpose. A device that fits under a suit needs a very small battery, and it is worn all day and during sleep, so wearing it cannot be optional. That is why the wearable has no AI, no storage and no link to Earth. It reads its sensors and sends small bursts to the spacecraft, which is always close by. Alerts come back as the reply to each burst, so the device never has to stay listening. In the real product a burst goes out every 5 seconds. The least work on the device leaves the most battery for the astronaut.

A private network that every connection goes through. The spacecraft hub runs on Cloudflare. Wearables only talk to the hub, and every request must carry a secret key that is checked before anything is accepted. The hub screen draws the whole network as a tree, with a color for each kind of traffic, so a crew member can see what is connected and where each message is going.

A database as the source of truth. Cloudflare D1 stores the astronauts and their baselines, every reading, every alert and an outbox for Earth. Nothing important lives only on a device or on a screen.

Two AIs, with rules in charge. Fixed rules trigger alerts, so a slow or wrong AI answer can never block a "go back in" alert. Workers AI explains alerts and writes daily summaries. A second AI runs locally on board, answers the astronaut's questions from the live numbers, double-checks summaries, and rejects any wording that changes a number. It never gives a diagnosis.

A link to Earth built to fail. Cutting the link stops only the Cloudflare-to-NASA leg. Records wait in the database, NASA retries every 3 seconds, and every retry is logged. On restore they flush to NASA, NASA confirms what it saved, anything unconfirmed is sent again, and a checker confirms the databases agree.

The science

The question: how can we reliably track individualized astronaut health anomalies in constrained, disconnected environments?

Why the data fits. Normal is different for every person, so a fixed threshold is the wrong tool. Each astronaut's pre-flight medical report, uploaded as a PDF or typed in, becomes their personal baseline. Live vitals are judged against that baseline, and NASA spaceflight research decides when a deviation matters. A drop in blood oxygen, a heart rate well above that person's resting level, or a radiation spike becomes critical only relative to the baseline and to the limits in NASA-STD-3001.

  • OSDR studies (for example OSD-52, OSD-816 and OSD-992) ground the risk models for bone loss, cardiovascular stress, immune response and radiation, and are linked from the NASA view.
  • Curiosity RAD gives real measured radiation doses, replayed along the simulated mission, so dose numbers follow real physics.
  • DONKI supplies real space weather events (flares, CMEs, solar energetic particle events) that trigger live radiation alerts. A replay control injects a real past event, so the demo does not depend on the sun.

What is new here

An offline-first, dual-AI design. All intelligence lives on the spacecraft. The wearable has no AI and no storage, so it stays light. Two AIs work next to each other: Workers AI on Cloudflare explains alerts and writes summaries, and a local on-board agent converses with the crew and answers from the live numbers without needing a connection to Earth. Fixed rules, not AI, trigger alerts, so an AI failure can never silence a warning.

A store-and-forward outbox that proves nothing is lost. Records queue through a blackout and flush to NASA on restore, NASA confirms what it saved, and a checker confirms the databases agree. You can watch it happen by pressing Cut the link and Restore the link.

How is our project creative?

  • sensors and more smarts to the body. We took them off. The wearable has no AI and no storage, and all the intelligence lives on the spacecraft, so the device can be small, light and worn all day.
  • We treat the blackout as normal, not as an error. The system is offline-first. When the link to Earth drops, records wait in an outbox and sync on restore. We made that visible and testable with a Cut the link and Restore the link button, a 3-2-1 retry counter and a checker that says the databases agree.
  • AI explains, rules decide. Two AIs work on board, Workers AI and a local agent. Fixed rules trigger every alert, and the agent rejects any wording that changes a number, so an AI mistake can never hide a danger.
  • A personal baseline from the astronaut's own pre-flight report. Upload the PDF or type the values, and every reading is judged against that person, not against an average.
  • A language of vibration. A spacewalker cannot easily look at a screen, so each alert type has its own buzz pattern. Three long buzzes means go back inside now.
  • Data you can see and trust. A 3D body highlights stressed organs, the hub draws the private network as a living tree with a color for each kind of traffic, and every number is labelled measured, reference, simulated or modeled.
  • A whole mission in one demo. One real minute is one mission day, so judges watch sleep, a spacewalk, a solar event, a link failure and a report to NASA in a few minutes.
  • Built as a research record. What the system collects is designed to be reused: how each body handled the mission becomes evidence for planning the next one.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Battery and comfort. The wearable must fit under a suit and be worn all day and during sleep, so it has a very small battery and does the least possible work.
  • Distance and blackouts. Signals take up to 22 minutes one way to Mars and the link can drop, so support and storage had to work without Earth.
  • Safety. MedVital gives no diagnosis. Rules trigger alerts, the AI only explains, and a slow or wrong AI answer can never block a go-back-inside alert. Unusual readings are double-checked to tell a sensor glitch from a real problem.
  • Individual differences. One astronaut's normal resting heart rate is another's warning sign, so every alert is relative to that person's baseline.
  • Spacewalks and radiation. Solar events can arrive while an astronaut is outside, so the system tracks dose per spacewalk and per mission against NASA-STD-3001 limits and warns before a limit is reached.
  • Long-term health, not only emergencies. We track sleep, exercise (needed to fight bone and muscle loss), onboard blood and urine tests, and stress trends, covering all four risks: radiation, bone, heart and behavioral health.
  • Privacy and security. Medical data moves only over a private network. Every request needs a secret key, and no key or account id is stored in the repository or on any laptop.
  • Trust in the data. Real NASA data where it exists, and honest labels where we simulate or model.
  • Practicality of the demo. The simulation runs on three laptops or one, can run with a local model, and uses a one-command setup, so it can be shown anywhere.
  • Future value. Keeping a complete record per astronaut gives NASA evidence to plan future missions.

How it is built

MedVital is a distributed web simulation: an astronaut station, a spacecraft hub and a NASA receiver that can run on three laptops.

  • Astronaut station: an interactive 3D anatomical body (three.js, BodyParts3D) that highlights stressed organs, live telemetry charts, and a local AI chat assistant.
  • Spacecraft hub: a Python backend (mission clock, crew simulator, rules, outbox sync, scheduler) and a dashboard that draws the private network live.
  • Cloudflare: a Worker with a D1 database and Workers AI, locked with a secret key.
  • NASA receiver: Flask and SQLite, with the flight surgeon's screen and the daily summaries.
  • Quality: automated tests for the backend and the 3D dashboard, and one command (python start.py --fresh) that installs and runs everything. Built in VS Code and GitHub Codespaces.

How we used Cloudflare

  • Workers: the Worker receives the spacecraft's day-end batches and urgent alerts and holds the link switch for Cut the link and Restore the link.
  • D1: keeps every record and the outbox for Earth, so nothing important lives only on a device.
  • Workers AI: words alerts and daily summaries and answers the on-board agent's questions, and any answer that changes a number is rejected.
  • Cron trigger: fetches NASA DONKI space weather into D1 every 30 minutes.
  • Private network and secrets: every request needs a secret key checked in the Worker, and no account id, token or key sits in the repository or on any laptop.
  • Checker: the hub and NASA report in every 3 seconds, the Worker marks silent parts as down and checks that the spacecraft, D1 and NASA agree.
  • Quick tunnel (optional): publishes the hub so a phone can open the astronaut screen and really vibrate.

A research record for the future

MedVital is also a study of how astronauts' bodies handle a mission. Every day produces a full report per astronaut: vitals, sleep, onboard blood and urine tests, time spent outside, radiation dose, alerts and a summary, shown next to their pre-flight baseline. That is why we track sleep, bone-loss tests and every spacewalk. NASA's flight surgeon can pick any astronaut and any day and see exactly how they compared with their baseline. All of it stays in the record, so the data from this mission can inform planning for the next one.

Why it is a simulation, and why one minute is one day. We built the mission as a simulation so we can explain it live. The demo clock runs 1 real minute as 1 mission day: days 1 to 8 are the cruise to Mars, the crew lands on day 9, and spacewalks start on day 10. In one short demo you can watch sleep, exercise, a spacewalk, a solar event, a link failure and a day-end report to NASA. To make that watchable, each simulated wearable sends a reading every second. The real product would send a small burst every 5 seconds.

Watch it in 60 seconds

  1. Spacecraft hub. The private network as a tree, with a color for each kind of traffic and a legend under the drawing.
  2. Astronaut screen (Maya Okafor). Her 3D body, live. Click any box to see what the number means for her.
  3. Spacewalk. Press Leave the spacecraft and watch the radiation level rise, then press Go back inside.
  4. Ask the assistant. "My head hurts" gets common spaceflight causes with sources, a check of her live numbers and what to try, never a diagnosis, plus Send to flight surgeon.
  5. Cut the link, then restore it. Watch the outbox grow, then drain, and the databases agree.
  6. NASA screen. Pick an astronaut and a day for the full report, pre-flight versus now, alerts and upcoming events.

NASA data we used, and how honest we are about it

We use three NASA datasets, and none of them needs a login: Curiosity RAD for real radiation doses, DONKI for real space weather, and OSDR for the research behind each risk. Every number on screen carries a label that says where it came from.

  • Radiation dose rate (measured): real Curiosity RAD observations (NASA PDS, cruise 2011–12 and surface 2012), replayed at that point of the simulated mission and multiplied by RAD's measured quality factor (3.82 cruise, 3.05 surface).
  • Space weather (measured): real NASA DONKI records (May–June 2024): flares, CMEs, solar particle events and storms, placed on the mission calendar. They trigger live radiation alerts.
  • Research behind each risk (reference): NASA OSDR studies (for example OSD-52, OSD-816, OSD-992) for bone loss, cardiovascular stress, immune response and radiation, linked from the NASA view.
  • Heart rate, blood oxygen, breathing, temperature and test results (simulated): generated around each astronaut's pre-flight report.
  • Bone density (modeled): modeled from the loss rates in Sibonga et al. (2015) that the 3D body cites.

Alert thresholds follow NASA-STD-3001: 600 mSv career and 250 mSv per solar event. The spacewalk budget and heart-rate allowances are demo settings.

Honest limits

MedVital is not a medical device and gives no diagnosis. The four astronauts and their pre-flight reports are fictional. Vitals and test results are simulated around those reports, and bone density is modeled. What is real is the NASA data behind radiation and space weather, the architecture (wearable, private network, database, link to Earth), and the behavior when the link is cut and restored.


  • We flipped the usual design. Most health trackers add more
